new_statements.quote: In Tangkhul languages, stress is always predictable. Only roots bear stress, and prefixes never bear stress. The preferred stress pattern, for a word (and foot), is iambic or anapestic. That is to say, a stem usually consists of a stressed (heavy syllable) root and one or two unstressed (light syllable) prefixes. Suffixes that are not a stem in their own right are not stressed, but these often form part of the same stressed syllable as the root.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is fully predictable from morphology: the root syllable carries the stress; the one or two prefix syllables that precede it (with reduced vowels) are unstressed, so the word/foot is iambic or anapestic (stress on the last syllable of the prefix+root stem); non-stem suffixes are unstressed. Stated for 'Tangkhul languages' as a group (Standard Tangkhul/Ukhrul, Kachai, Huishu data), not from Khangoi data.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The statement is group-level; Khangoi itself is known only from McCulloch's 1859 wordlist, from which (Mortensen 2003 p. 5) 'only a little knowledge about the phonology.. may be deduced'. Prefix tone is largely predictable but may be contrastive in numerals and nouns (sec. 3.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level (prefix + root [+ suffix]); the author speaks of 'a word (and foot)'. Group-level claim for Tangkhulic languages; Khangoi is placed in the group's 'Southern' branch on 19th-century wordlist evidence only. No Khangoi-specific phonological description exists in any opened source.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog khan1277 'Southern Tangkhul Naga' = the lect of Khangoi (Khanggoi, McCulloch's 'Khoonggoee') village, 'a few hours' journey to the east of Ukhrul' (Grierson 1903 p. 472), attested only by McCulloch's 1859 wordlist (+ Brown 1837's 'Northern Tangkhul', which Mortensen 2003 Fig. 3 groups with Khangoi under 'Southern'); Glottolog's own page mislabels it 'Northern Tangkhul Naga' in the comment. Brown's 'Southern Tangkhul' is a Kuki-Chin language, not this one. Grambank codes khan1277 from Takhellambam 2014 'Descriptive grammar of Kabrang Tangkhul' (Kabrang village), i.e. Grambank equates Kabrang Tangkhul with khan1277 -- an identity decision not confirmed by Glottolog. The quoted stress statement (Mortensen 2003) is for the Tangkhul group as a whole, built on Standard Tangkhul/Ukhrul (tang1336), Kachai and Huishu (nort3286) data; the same passage is already filed for nort3286, nort3287 and tang1336.

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (1903). Linguistic Survey of India, vol. III pt. 2: Tibeto-Burman family, Bodo, Naga and Kachin groups. Calcutta: Office of the Superintendent of Government Printing. Section 'Luhupa or Luppa' pp. 463 ff., 'Khangoi' p. 472.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p. 463: 'Three, -- Tangkhul, Phadang, and Khangoi have been recorded.' p. 472 'KHANGOI': 'It is a few hours' journey to the east of Ukhrul. Damant estimates the number of speakers at 300. McCulloch has given us a vocabulary of it, which partly agrees with Brown's Northern Tangkhul. So far as can be judged from this vocabulary, this language has much more of a Kuki complexion than the Tangkhul of Ukhrul.' Authorities listed: Brown 1837, McCulloch 1859 (Khoongoee vocabulary, App. I pp. v ff.), Damant 1880. Only the standard word list is given; no pronunciation or accent note for Khangoi.

sources.citation: McCulloch, W. (1859). Account of the Valley of Munnipore and of the Hill Tribes; with a comparative vocabulary of the Munnipore and other languages. Selections from the Records of the Government of India (Foreign Department) No. 27. Calcutta: Bengal Printing Company. [Glottolog reference; the only primary data on Khangoi]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Appendix No. I is a 'Comparative Vocabulary of the Munniporee, Undro, Sengmai, Chairel, Meeyang, Koupooee Pooeeron, Koupooee Songboo, Quoireng, Khoonggoee, Phudang, Koopome, Tukaimee, Muram, Murring, Anal Namfau, Kookie, Burmese and Shan languages' (Lt. Stewart's word and sentence list); the only pronunciation note is a vowel/consonant key ('a is pronounced as in Italian', 'th always has the h aspirated', etc.). No remark on accent, stress or intonation for Khoonggoee or any language (a full-text search for stress/accent/intonation/emphasis: no relevant hit).
